<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm_main_pseudo_telepathy}
    For every $n\geq 2$, there exist unsatisfiable linear constraint systems modulo $n$ whose game admits a perfect quantum strategy over $\mathbb C^{2n}$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm_ain}
For every $n\geq2$,  the structure $\mathbf{Lin}_n$ is pseudo-telepathic over $\mathbb C^{2n}$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
A \emph{minion} ${\mathcal M}$ is a functor from the skeleton category of non-empty finite sets to
the category of non-empty sets. In other words, ${\mathcal M}$ is the disjoint union of non-empty sets ${\mathcal M}^{(\ell)}$ for $\ell\in\mathbb N$, equipped with operations $(\cdot)_{/\pi}:{\mathcal M}^{(\ell)}\to {\mathcal M}^{(\ell')}$ (known as \emph{minor operations}) for each pair of integers $\ell,\ell'\in\mathbb N$ and each map
$\pi:[\ell]\to [\ell']$, which must satisfy the following two conditions:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $M_{/\operatorname{id}}=M$ 
    for each $\ell\in\mathbb N$ and $M\in{\mathcal M}^{(\ell)}$, where $\operatorname{id}$ is the identity map on the set $[\ell]$;
    \item $(M_{/\pi})_{/\tilde\pi}=M_{/\tilde\pi\circ\pi}$
     for each $\ell,\ell',\ell''\in\mathbb N$, $M\in{\mathcal M}^{(\ell)}$, $\pi:[\ell]\to[\ell']$,
    and $\tilde\pi:[\ell']\to[\ell'']$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
A \emph{minion homomorphism} $\xi:{\mathcal M}\to{\mathcal N}$ is a natural transformation from ${\mathcal M}$ to ${\mathcal N}$. In other words, $\xi$ is a map from the underlying set of ${\mathcal M}$ to the underlying set of ${\mathcal N}$ that
\begin{itemize}
    \item preserves the arities---i.e., $\xi(M)\in{\mathcal N}^{(\ell)}$ if $M\in{\mathcal M}^{(\ell)}$;
    \item preserves the minors---i.e., $\xi(M_{/\pi})=\xi(M)_{/\pi}$ if $M\in{\mathcal M}^{(\ell)}$ and  $\pi:[\ell]\to[\ell']$.
\end{itemize}
We write ${\mathcal M}\to{\mathcal N}$ when such a $\xi$ exists; otherwise, we write ${\mathcal M}\not\to{\mathcal N}$. We also let a \textit{minion isomorphism} be a bijective minion homomorphism.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
For a finite-dimensional Hilbert space $H$, the \emph{quantum monad} ${\mathcal Q}_H$ is the minion whose $r$-ary set is
\begin{align*}
 {\mathcal Q}_H^{(r)}=
 \left\{(U_1,\dots,U_r)\in L_H^r:
    U_i\perp U_j\ (i\ne j),\quad \bigoplus_{i\in[r]}U_i=H\right\}.
\end{align*}
For $\pi:[r]\to[s]$, the corresponding minor operation is defined as follows:
\begin{align*}
 (U_1,\ldots,U_r)_{/\pi}
   =\left(\bigoplus_{i\in\pi^{-1}(1)}U_i,\dots,
           \bigoplus_{i\in\pi^{-1}(s)}U_i\right),
\end{align*}
where an empty sum is the space $\{0\}$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm_characterisation_PT}
A structure $\mathbf Y$ is pseudo-telepathic over a finite-dimensional Hilbert space
$H$ if, and only if,
${\mathcal Q}_H\not\to\operatorname{Pol}(\mathbf Y)$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
For $n\geq2$, define the minion $\mathsf{AIP}_n$ by
 $\mathsf{AIP}_n^{(r)}
   =\left\{\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb Z_n^r:
                  \mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{1}=1\right\}$,
with minor operations
$\mathbf{a}_{/\pi}
   =\left(\sum_{i\in\pi^{-1}(1)}a_i,\dots,
           \sum_{i\in\pi^{-1}(s)}a_i\right)$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop_pol}
For every $n\geq2$, the minions $\operatorname{Pol}(\mathbf{Lin}_n)$ and
$\mathsf{AIP}_n$ are isomorphic.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Consider the map $\xi: \mathsf{AIP}_n\to\operatorname{Pol}(\mathbf{Lin}_n)$ defined as follows: for each $r\in\mathbb N$, each $\mathbf{a}\in\mathsf{AIP}_n^{(r)}$, and each $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb Z_n^r$, $\xi(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x}=\sum_{i\in[r]}a_ix_i$. We claim that $\xi$ is well defined and it is a minion homomorphism.

First, we show that $\xi(\mathbf{a})$ is a polymorphism of $\mathbf{Lin}_n$. Note that $\xi(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{0})=0$, so $\xi(\mathbf{a})$ preserves $C_0$. Moreover, let $M$ be an $r\times 3$ matrix all of whose rows sum up to some $b\in\mathbb Z_n$. Then the application of $\xi(\mathbf{a})$ to the columns of $M$ yields $(\mathbf{a}^\top M\mathbf{e}_1,\mathbf{a}^\top M\mathbf{e}_2,\mathbf{a}^\top M\mathbf{e}_3)$, where $\mathbf{e}_i$ is the $i$-th standard unit vector. The sum of these values is $\mathbf{a}^\top M\mathbf{1}=b\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{1}=b$, so $\xi(\mathbf{a})$ preserves $R_b$ and is thus a polymorphism.

Take a map $\pi:[r]\to[s]$, and let $P_\pi$ be the $s\times r$ matrix whose $i$-th column is $\mathbf{e}_{\pi(i)}$. Note that
\begin{align*}
    \xi(\mathbf{a}_{/\pi})(\mathbf{x})
    =
    (P_\pi\mathbf{a})^\top\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{a}^\top P_{\pi}^\top\mathbf{x}=
    \xi(\mathbf{a})_{/\pi}(\mathbf{x}),
\end{align*}
so $\xi$ preserves minors and, thus, is a minion homomorphism.

Let now $f$ be an $r$-ary polymorphism of $\mathbf{Lin}_n$. Preservation of $C_0$ gives $f(\mathbf{0})=0$, and preservation of $R_0$ applied to $(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{0},-\mathbf{x})$ gives $f(-\mathbf{x})=-f(\mathbf{x})$. Hence, preservation of $R_0$ applied to $(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},-\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})$ gives $f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})=f(\mathbf{x})+f(\mathbf{y})$, so $f$ is a group homomorphism $\mathbb Z_n^r\to\mathbb Z_n$. Since the standard unit vectors generate $\mathbb Z_n^r$, it follows that 
    $f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{a}_f^\top\mathbf{x}$ for each $\mathbf{x}$, where $\mathbf{a}_f=(f(\mathbf{e}_1),\dots,f(\mathbf{e}_r))$. Clearly, $\mathbf{a}_f$ is uniquely determined. Furthermore, preservation of $R_1$ on $(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{0},\mathbf{0})$ gives $f(\mathbf{1})=1$, so $\mathbf{a}_f^\top\mathbf{1}=1$. Hence, $\mathbf{a}_f\in\mathsf{AIP}_n^{(r)}$. The map $\vartheta:\operatorname{Pol}(\mathbf{Lin}_n)\to\mathsf{AIP}_n$ given by $f\mapsto \mathbf{a}_f$  is the inverse of $\xi$, so $\xi$ is a minion isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space and let $A$ be an Abelian group.
An \emph{$A$-measure on the subspaces of $H$} is a
map $\mu:L_H\to A$ such that
\begin{align*}
 \mu(U\oplus V)=\mu(U)+\mu(V)\qquad\text{whenever }U\perp V.
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop_measure}
For every $n\geq2$ and every finite-dimensional Hilbert space $H$, a minion homomorphism ${\mathcal Q}_H\to\mathsf{AIP}_n$ exists
if, and only if, there is a $\mathbb Z_n$-measure $\mu$ on the subspaces of $H$ satisfying
$\mu(H)=1$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $\xi:{\mathcal Q}_H\to\mathsf{AIP}_n$ be a minion homomorphism, and define $\mu(U)=\xi((U,U^\perp))_1$ for each $U\in L_H$. For any $U\perp V\in L_H$, write $\xi((U,V,(U\oplus V)^\perp))=(a,b,1-a-b)$. Since $\xi$ is a minion homomorphism, we have that $\mu(U)=a$, $\mu(V)=b$, and $\mu(U\oplus V)=a+b$. Hence, $\mu$ is a $\mathbb Z_n$-measure on the subspaces of $H$. Moreover, $\xi(H)=1$ and, thus, $\xi((H,\{0\}))=(1,0)$, which means that $\mu(H)=1$.

Conversely, suppose $\mu$ is a $\mathbb Z_n$-measure  on the subspaces of $H$ satisfying $\mu(H)=1$. For a tuple $\mathbf{u}=(U_1,\dots,U_r)\in{\mathcal Q}_H^{(r)}$, we let $\xi(\mathbf{u})=(\mu(U_1),\dots,\mu(U_r))\in\mathbb Z_n^r$. Since the $U_i$'s are mutually orthogonal, the fact that $\mu$ is a measure on the subspaces of $H$ implies that 
    \begin{align*}\sum_{i\in[r]}\mu(U_i)=\mu\left(\bigoplus_{i\in[r]}U_i\right)=\mu(H)=1,
    \end{align*}
    so $\xi(\mathbf{u})\in\mathsf{AIP}_n^{(r)}$. To show that $\xi$ is a minion homomorphism, take a map $\pi:[r]\to[s]$, and observe that
    \begin{align*}
        \xi(\mathbf{u}_{/\pi})
        &=
        \xi\left(\bigoplus_{i\in\pi^{-1}(1)}U_i,\dots,\bigoplus_{i\in\pi^{-1}(s)}U_i\right)
        =
        \left(\mu\left(\bigoplus_{i\in\pi^{-1}(1)}U_i\right),\dots,\mu\left(\bigoplus_{i\in\pi^{-1}(s)}U_i\right)\right)\\
        &=\left(\sum_{i\in\pi^{-1}(1)}\mu(U_i),\dots,\sum_{i\in\pi^{-1}(s)}\mu(U_i)\right)
        =
        \xi(\mathbf{u})_{/\pi},
    \end{align*}
    where the third equality uses that subspaces with distinct indices are mutually orthogonal and, thus, $\mu$ behaves additively on them.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{lem_hjs}
For every $n\geq2$, every $\mathbb Z_n$-measure $\mu$ on the subspaces of $\mathbb R^{2n}$ satisfies $\mu(\mathbb R^{2n})=0$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem_complexification}
For every $n\in\mathbb N$, there exists a minion homomorphism ${\mathcal Q}_{\mathbb R^n}\to{\mathcal Q}_{\mathbb C^n}$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
For any $U\in L_{\mathbb R^n}$, consider its complexification $U^{\mathbb C}=U\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C\in L_{\mathbb C^n}$. Let $\xi:{\mathcal Q}_{\mathbb R^n}\to{\mathcal Q}_{\mathbb C^n}$ be the map defined by $(U_1,\dots,U_r)\mapsto (U_1^\mathbb C,\dots,U_r^\mathbb C)$. We claim that $\xi$ is a minion homomorphism. First, for $i\neq j$, since $U_i\perp U_j$, we have that $U_i^\mathbb C\perp U_j^\mathbb C$. Moreover,
    \begin{align*}
        \bigoplus_{i\in[r]}U_i^\mathbb C=\bigoplus_{i\in[r]}(U_i\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C)=(\bigoplus_{i\in[r]}U_i)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C=\mathbb R^n\otimes_\mathbb R\mathbb C=\mathbb C^n,
        \end{align*}
        so $\xi$ is a well-defined map from ${\mathcal Q}_{\mathbb R^n}$ to ${\mathcal Q}_{\mathbb C^n}$. The fact that $\xi$ preserves minors is straightforward.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Suppose by contradiction that ${\mathcal Q}_{\mathbb C^{2n}}\to\operatorname{Pol}(\mathbf{Lin}_n)$. Composing this minion homomorphism with  those from~\Cref{prop_pol} and Lemma~$\ref{lem_complexification}$ yields ${\mathcal Q}_{\mathbb R^{2n}}\to\mathsf{AIP}_n$. We then deduce from~\Cref{prop_measure} that there exists a $\mathbb Z_n$-measure $\mu$ on the subspaces of $\mathbb R^{2n}$ satisfying $\mu(\mathbb R^{2n})=1$, contradicting~\Cref{lem_hjs}.
 
    Hence, ${\mathcal Q}_{\mathbb C^{2n}}\not\to\operatorname{Pol}(\mathbf{Lin}_n)$, and it follows from~\Cref{thm_characterisation_PT} that $\mathbf{Lin}_n$ is pseudo-telepathic over $\mathbb C^{2n}$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor_unbounded_width}
    A structure $\mathbf Y$ is pseudo-telepathic if, and only if, it has unbounded width.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
